input.rationale: Corrected the verify question's timing premise rather than leaving a vague one on record. The account previously attributed the successor-overlap condition to a leader stall or a window of ElectionTimeout - LeaderLeaseTimeout; reading the loops shows ElectionTimeout governs only a candidate's retry, the follower's election trigger is HeartbeatTimeout with randomization to [H, 2H), and the leader's lease check granularity is max(10ms, LeaderLeaseTimeout - maxDiff). Under the documented defaults the leader therefore leaves office about 500ms before the earliest campaign, and the windows can only touch when LeaderLeaseTimeout == HeartbeatTimeout, which validation permits, where the boundary comparison (diff <= leaseTimeout) and the 10ms check floor open an exposure of about 10ms plus the election itself. The question's evidence, executions and defect claim are unchanged; this update corrects the limitation and the gap answer and records the trigger semantics as a reusable Behaviour.

knowledge.statement: A follower attempts an election after HeartbeatTimeout without contact from a leader, and ElectionTimeout governs only a candidate's retry. runFollower arms heartbeatTimer with randomTimeout(HeartbeatTimeout) and campaigns when the time since last contact is at least HeartbeatTimeout, while runCandidate arms its timer with randomTimeout(ElectionTimeout) and simply restarts the election when it fires. randomTimeout(v) returns v plus a random fraction of v, so a campaign begins in [H, 2H). Correspondingly ValidateConfig requires LeaderLeaseTimeout <= HeartbeatTimeout <= ElectionTimeout, and the leader's own lease check runs every max(minCheckInterval, LeaderLeaseTimeout - maxDiff) with minCheckInterval = 10ms, stepping down at the first check whose voter contact age exceeds LeaderLeaseTimeout; the comparison is diff <= leaseTimeout, so a check at exactly the boundary still counts the voter as contacted.
knowledge.conditions: The default follower and leader loops in this snapshot, with pre-vote enabled or disabled; the numbers quoted are for a configuration accepted by ValidateConfig, and the exposure analysis assumes in-memory or low-latency RPCs.

interpretations.rationale: VerifyLeader's documented role is to ensure this peer is still the leader so that stale data is not returned from the FSM. The question was whether its success establishes voter-majority contact; the execution says it does not. In the retained run of the three-partition probe, the leader whose only reachable peer was the non-voter returned success in 0ms while its own latest configuration reported three voters, one non-voter and a quorum size of 2, and the leader was still in Leader state (parsed event index 1); the control partition that kept one voter reachable also returned success, which shows the harness does observe a genuine acknowledgement path (index 3); the control partition with no reachable peer did not return success at all, returning 'leadership lost while committing log' after 202ms with the node in Follower state, so the leader cannot reach the threshold on its own vote and the non-voter acknowledgement is what satisfied it in the first case (index 5). All three declared comparisons hold with the setup event matched as admission (correlations 1->0, 3->2, 5->4). The source explains the mechanism: verifyLeader asks every entry of leaderState.replState to acknowledge, startStopReplication creates such an entry for every configured server except the leader without consulting Suffrage, any successful AppendEntries or InstallSnapshot reply from such a peer calls notifyAll(true) and increments verifyFuture.votes, and the threshold compared against is quorumSize(), counted over voters alone. The same package treats voter eligibility strictly in its other leadership tests: checkLeaderLease does not count a non-voter, requestVote refuses a candidate that holds no vote, and quorumSize itself counts only voters, so the verify path is the outlier rather than a deliberate relaxation. The consequence for reads stays bounded and is not what this receipt measures. The leader's lease is voter-only, and both Config.Validate and ReloadConfig enforce LeaderLeaseTimeout <= HeartbeatTimeout <= ElectionTimeout, so the old leader is normally removed before a voter majority elects a successor; the no-peer control is exactly that lease firing at 202ms with a 200ms lease. What the receipt does establish is the weaker but unconditional part: for an interval in which the leader exchanged nothing with any other voter, VerifyLeader reports success, so a caller relying on that call for read consistency is really relying on the lease timer rather than on the acknowledgements VerifyLeader collected. The same file shows the omission is not a considered relaxation of voter eligibility: electSelf and preElectSelf build the very same voter-sized threshold, and both iterate the leader's latest configuration asking only servers whose Suffrage is Voter, so a candidate neither solicits nor counts a non-voter's grant even though nothing on the granting side stops a non-voter from granting a vote if it were asked. Only the verify path asks every replication peer. That contrast is recorded as its own Behaviour so the finding is not reused without it, and it turns the question's answer from 'the success signal is weaker than its documentation' into 'the success signal contradicts the eligibility rule the same decisions use everywhere else'.

knowledge.statement: The leader's own leadership lease is computed over voters only: checkLeaderLease counts itself plus those servers in configurations.latest whose Suffrage is Voter and whose followerReplication last contact is within LeaderLeaseTimeout, and steps down when that count is below quorumSize(). knowledge.statement: LeadershipTransferToServer accepts a non-voter target and reports success without transferring leadership to it. The leader resolves the requested ID in leaderState.replState, which contains an entry for every configured server except the leader (startStopReplication creates one per server without consulting Suffrage) and only errors with 'cannot find replication state' when no entry exists. The selected target is sent TimeoutNow, which sets it to Candidate and marks candidateFromLeadershipTransfer; that flag makes runCandidate skip pre-vote, so the target sends a real RequestVote carrying the next term. A voter handling that request adopts the higher term and becomes a follower before it reaches the hasVote check, which then refuses the vote because the candidate holds no vote; the candidate therefore cannot win. When the old leader observes the higher term it steps down, the transfer goroutine's leftLeaderLoop branch responds nil, and the caller sees success. By contrast LeadershipTransfer with no explicit target picks through pickServer, which skips every server whose Suffrage is not Voter.
knowledge.conditions: Protocol version >= 3 (otherwise LeadershipTransferToServer returns ErrUnsupportedProtocol), a cluster whose latest configuration at the leader contains the named server with Suffrage other than Voter, and pre-vote enabled or disabled (the transfer path skips pre-vote either way). The named server must be reachable from the leader, otherwise the leader reports a TimeoutNow failure instead.

knowledge.statement: A leadership transfer requested for a non-voter leaves the cluster without a leader until a voter wins the next election, while the call itself has already reported success. knowledge.conditions: Cluster of three voters plus one non-voter joined through AddNonvoter, protocol version >= 3, all peers reachable, pre-vote left at its default, and a single process with in-memory transports; the target is chosen by its suffrage in the leader's latest configuration, not by any observed result.

knowledge.statement: Election vote solicitation is restricted to voters, unlike the verify path in the same file. electSelf and preElectSelf both iterate configurations.latest.Servers and act only when server.Suffrage == Voter: the local server records a vote for itself and every other server is asked with a RequestVote or RequestPreVote RPC, while non-voters are skipped altogether, so no non-voter grant is ever counted toward the voter-sized quorum they compare against. interpretations.rationale: The question was whether LeadershipTransferToServer reports a transfer that the named server can complete when that server is a non-voter, and what happens to leadership while it cannot. The execution answers the first half directly. In the control case naming a voter (parsed indices 0 and 1) the call returned nil and the requested server was Leader at the endpoint while the previous leader was Follower, so the call does perform real transfers. In the case naming the non-voter (parsed indices 2 and 3, setup event index 2 matched as admission) the same call returned nil while the requested server was never observed as Leader within 1500ms and finished as Follower; the previous leader was not Leader at the endpoint and the maximum term across the cluster had risen from 2 to 4, with the same server holding leadership at term 4, which a Raft leader cannot do without having stepped down and won a later election. The source explains the mechanism as predicted. The leader resolves the requested ID only through leaderState.replState, which startStopReplication populates for every configured server except the leader without consulting Suffrage, so a non-voter passes and receives TimeoutNow; timeoutNow sets it to Candidate and marks candidateFromLeadershipTransfer, a flag that by design suppresses pre-vote, so it sends a real RequestVote carrying the next term. Each voter adopts the higher term and becomes a follower before reaching the hasVote check, which then refuses the vote because the candidate holds no vote, so the requested server can never collect a grant. The old leader learns of the higher term, steps down, and its transfer goroutine reports success from the leftLeaderLoop branch, so the caller is told the transfer succeeded while leadership has in fact left it for a server it did not choose, or returned to it in a later term. That mismatch is the defect: for the documented purpose of handing leadership over, a success result that the named target can never satisfy leaves the caller unable to distinguish a completed handover from a self-inflicted leadership interruption. The liveness side is bounded rather than unbounded and this receipt does not measure it, since leadership was sampled only at the end of the observation window; the revised probe samples every millisecond and records the leaderless samples. No data loss is claimed: committed entries stay committed and a voter is elected afterwards.
